L24: # DeleteFile function (winbase.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Deletes an existing file.
L33: 
L34: To perform this operation as a transacted operation, use the 【5†DeleteFileTransacted】 function.
L35: 
L36: ## Syntax
L37: 
L38:     `BOOL DeleteFile(
L39:       [in] LPCTSTR lpFileName
L40:     );
L41:     `
L42: ## Parameters
L43: 
L44: `[in] lpFileName`
L45: 
L46: The name of the file to be deleted.
L47: 
L48: By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. For more information, see 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】.
L49: 
L50: Tip
L51: 
L52: Starting with Windows 10, Version 1607, you can opt-in to remove the MAX_PATH limitation without prepending "\\?\". See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】 for details.
L53: ## Return value
L54: 
L55: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L56: 
L57: If the function fails, the return value is zero (0). To get extended error information, call 【7†GetLastError】.
L58: ## Remarks
L59: 
L60: If an application attempts to delete a file that does not exist, the DeleteFile function fails with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND. If the file is a read-only file, the function fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED.
L61: 
L62: The following list identifies some tips for deleting, removing, or closing files:
L63:   * To delete a read-only file, first you must remove the read-only attribute.
L64:   * To delete or rename a file, you must have either delete permission on the file, or delete child permission in the parent directory.
L65:   * To recursively delete the files in a directory, use the 【8†SHFileOperation】 function.
L66:   * To remove an empty directory, use the 【9†RemoveDirectory】 function.
L67:   * To close an open file, use the 【10†CloseHandle】 function.
L68: If you set up a directory with all access except delete and delete child, and the access control lists (ACL) of new files are inherited, then you can create a file without being able to delete it. However, then you can create a file, and then get all the access you request on the handle that is returned to you at the time you create the file.
L69: If you request delete permission at the time you create a file, you can delete or rename the file with that handle, but not with any other handle. For more information, see 【11†File Security and Access Rights】.
L70: 
L71: The DeleteFile function fails if an application attempts to delete a file that has other open handles that were opened without FILE_SHARE_DELETE, or that is memory-mapped.
L72: The DeleteFile function marks a file for deletion on close. Therefore, the file deletion does not occur until the last handle to the file is closed. Subsequent calls to 【12†CreateFile】 to open the file fail with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED.
L73: 
L74: Symbolic link behavior—
L75: 
L76: If the path points to a symbolic link, the symbolic link is deleted, not the target. To delete a target, you must call 【12†CreateFile】 and specify FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE.
L77: In Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, this function is supported by the following technologies.
L78: 
L79: Technology  | Supported
L80: --- | ---
L81: Server Message Block (SMB) 3.0 protocol  | Yes
L82: SMB 3.0 Transparent Failover (TFO)  | Yes
L83: SMB 3.0 with Scale-out File Shares (SO)  | Yes
L84: Cluster Shared Volume File System (CsvFS)  | Yes
L85: Resilient File System (ReFS)  | Yes
L86: #### Examples
L87: 
L88: For an example, see 【13†Locking and Unlocking Byte Ranges in Files】.
L89:

L91: 
L92: Requirement  | Value
L93: --- | ---
L94: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L95: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps | UWP apps]

L24: # File Access Rights Constants
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: The valid access rights for files and directories include the DELETE, READ_CONTROL, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, and SYNCHRONIZE 【5†standard access rights】. The following table lists the access rights that are specific to files and directories.
L32: 
L33: Constant/value  | Description
L34: --- | ---
L35: 
L36: FILE_ADD_FILE
L37: 2
L38:  | For a directory, the right to create a file in the directory.
L39: 
L40: FILE_ADD_SUBDIRECTORY
L41: 4
L42:  | For a directory, the right to create a subdirectory.
L43: FILE_ALL_ACCESS
L44:  | All possible access rights for a file.
L45: 
L46: FILE_APPEND_DATA
L47: 4
L48:  | For a file object, the right to append data to the file. (For local files, write operations will not overwrite existing data if this flag is specified without FILE_WRITE_DATA.) For a directory object, the right to create a subdirectory (FILE_ADD_SUBDIRECTORY).
L49: 
L50: FILE_CREATE_PIPE_INSTANCE
L51: 4
L52:  | For a named pipe, the right to create a pipe.
L53: FILE_DELETE_CHILD
L54: 64 (0x40)
L55:  | For a directory, the right to delete a directory and all the files it contains, including read-only files.
L56: 
L57: FILE_EXECUTE
L58: 32 (0x20)
L59:  | For a native code file, the right to execute the file. This access right given to scripts may cause the script to be executable, depending on the script interpreter.
L60: 
L61: FILE_LIST_DIRECTORY
L62: 1
L63:  | For a directory, the right to list the contents of the directory.
L64: 
L65: FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES
L66: 128 (0x80)
L67:  | The right to read file attributes.
L68: FILE_READ_DATA
L69: 1
L70:  | For a file object, the right to read the corresponding file data. For a directory object, the right to read the corresponding directory data.
L71: 
L72: FILE_READ_EA
L73: 8
L74:  | The right to read extended file attributes.
L75: 
L76: FILE_TRAVERSE
L77: 32 (0x20)
L78:  | For a directory, the right to traverse the directory. By default, users are assigned the BYPASS_TRAVERSE_CHECKING 【6†privilege】, which ignores the FILE_TRAVERSE 【7†access right】. See the remarks in 【8†File Security and Access Rights】 for more information.
L79: FILE_WRITE_ATTRIBUTES
L80: 256 (0x100)
L81:  | The right to write file attributes.
L82: 
L83: FILE_WRITE_DATA
L84: 2
L85:  | For a file object, the right to write data to the file. For a directory object, the right to create a file in the directory (FILE_ADD_FILE).
L86: 
L87: FILE_WRITE_EA
L88: 16 (0x10)
L89:  | The right to write extended file attributes.
L90: 
L91: STANDARD_RIGHTS_READ
L92:  | Includes READ_CONTROL, which is the right to read the information in the file or directory object's security descriptor. This does not include the information in the SACL.
L93: STANDARD_RIGHTS_WRITE
L94:  | Same as STANDARD_RIGHTS_READ.

L24: # RemoveDirectoryW function (fileapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Deletes an existing empty directory.
L33: 
L34: To perform this operation as a transacted operation, use the 【5†RemoveDirectoryTransacted】 function.
L35: 
L36: ## Syntax
L37: 
L38:     `BOOL RemoveDirectoryW(
L39:       [in] LPCWSTR lpPathName
L40:     );
L41:     `
L42: ## Parameters
L43: 
L44: `[in] lpPathName`
L45: 
L46: The path of the directory to be removed. This path must specify an empty directory, and the calling process must have delete access to the directory.
L47: 
L48: By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. For more information, see 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】.
L49: 
L50: Tip
L51: Starting with Windows 10, Version 1607, you can opt-in to remove the MAX_PATH limitation without prepending "\\?\". See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】 for details.
L52: ## Return value
L53: 
L54: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L55: 
L56: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call 【7†GetLastError】.
L57: ## Remarks
L58: 
L59: The RemoveDirectory function marks a directory for deletion on close. Therefore, the directory is not removed until the last handle to the directory is closed.
L60: 
L61: To recursively delete the files in a directory, use the 【8†SHFileOperation】 function.
L62: RemoveDirectory can be used to remove a directory junction. Since the target directory and its contents will remain accessible through its canonical path, the target directory itself is not affected by removing a junction which targets it. For this reason, when lpPathName refers to a directory junction, RemoveDirectory will remove the specified link regardless of whether the target directory is empty or not. For more information on junctions, see 【9†Hard Links and Junctions】.
L63: The use of POSIX delete causes the directory to be deleted while handles remain open. Subsequent calls to 【10†CreateDirectory】 to open the directory fail with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.
L64: 
L65: In Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, this function is supported by the following technologies.
L66: Technology  | Supported
L67: --- | ---
L68: Server Message Block (SMB) 3.0 protocol  | Yes
L69: SMB 3.0 Transparent Failover (TFO)  | Yes
L70: SMB 3.0 with Scale-out File Shares (SO)  | Yes
L71: Cluster Shared Volume File System (CsvFS)  | Yes
L72: Resilient File System (ReFS)  | Yes
L73: 
L74: Note
L75: The `fileapi.h` header defines RemoveDirectory as an alias that automatically selects the ANSI or Unicode version of this function based on the definition of the UNICODE preprocessor constant. Mixing usage of the encoding-neutral alias with code that is not encoding-neutral can lead to mismatches that result in compilation or runtime errors. For more information, see 【11†Conventions for Function Prototypes】.
L76: ## Requirements
L77: 
L78: Requirement  | Value
L79: --- | ---
L80: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L81: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L82: Target Platform  | Windows
L83: Header  | fileapi.h (include Windows.h)
L84: Library  | Kernel32.lib
L85: DLL  | Kernel32.dll

L24: # Job Objects
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: A job object allows groups of processes to be managed as a unit. Job objects are namable, securable, sharable objects that control attributes of the processes associated with them. Operations performed on a job object affect all processes associated with the job object. Examples include enforcing limits such as working set size and process priority or terminating all processes associated with a job.
L32:   * 【5†Creating Jobs】
L33:   * 【6†Managing Processes in Jobs】
L34:   * 【7†Job Limits and Notifications】
L35:   * 【8†Resource Accounting for Jobs】
L36:   * 【9†Managing Job Objects】
L37:   * 【10†Managing a Process Tree that Uses Job Objects】
L38: ## Creating Jobs
L39: 
L40: To create a job object, use the 【11†CreateJobObject】 function. When the job is created, no processes are associated with the job.
L41: 
L42: To associate a process with a job, use the 【12†AssignProcessToJobObject】 function. After a process is associated with a job, the association cannot be broken. A process can be associated with more than one job in a hierarchy of nested jobs. For more information, see 【13†Nested Jobs】.
L43: Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows XP with SP3, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista and Windows Server 2003: A process can be associated with only one job. Jobs cannot be nested. The ability to nest jobs was added in Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012.
L44: 
L45: You can specify a security descriptor for a job object when you call the 【11†CreateJobObject】 function. For more information, see 【14†Job Object Security and Access Rights】.
L46: ## Managing Processes in Jobs
L47: 
L48: After a process is associated with a job, by default any child processes it creates using 【15†CreateProcess】 are also associated with the job. (Child processes created using 【16†Win32_Process.Create】 are not associated with the job.) This default behavior can be changed by setting the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK or JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK for the job.
L49:   * If the job has the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK and the parent process was created with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag, then child processes of the parent process are not associated with the job.
L50:   * If the job has the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK, then child processes of any parent process associated with the job are not associated with the job. It is not necessary for parent processes to be created with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag.
L51: If the job is nested, the breakaway settings of parent jobs in the hierarchy affect whether child processes are associated with another job in the hierarchy. For more information, see 【13†Nested Jobs】.
L52: 
L53: To determine if a process is running in a job, use the 【17†IsProcessInJob】 function.
L54: 
L55: To terminate all processes currently associated with a job object, use the 【18†TerminateJobObject】 function.
L56: ## Job Limits and Notifications
L57: 
L58: A job can enforce limits such as working set size, process priority, and end-of-job time limit on each process that is associated with the job. If a process associated with a job attempts to increase its working set size or process priority from the limit established by the job, the function calls succeed but are silently ignored. A job can also set limits that trigger a notification when they are exceeded but allow the job to continue to run.
L59: To set limits for a job, use the 【19†SetInformationJobObject】 function. For a list of possible limits that can be set for a job, see the following topics:
L60: 
L61:   * 【20†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION】
L62:   * 【21†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_UI_RESTRICTIONS】
L63:   * 【22†JOBOBJECT_CPU_RATE_CONTROL_INFORMATION】
L64:   * 【23†JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION】
L65:   * 【24†JOBOBJECT_NOTIFICATION_LIMIT_INFORMATION】
L66: Security limits must be set individually for each process associated with a job object. For more information, see 【25†Process Security and Access Rights】.
L67: 
L68: Windows XP with SP3 and Windows Server 2003: The 【19†SetInformationJobObject】 function can be used to set security limitations for all processes associated with a job object. Starting with Windows Vista, security limits must be set individually for each process associated with a job object.
L69: If the job is nested, parent jobs in the hierarchy influence the limit that is enforced for the job. For more information, see 【13†Nested Jobs】.
L70: If the job has an associated I/O completion port, it can receive notifications when certain job limits are exceeded. The system sends messages to the completion port when a limit is exceeded or certain other events occur. To associate a completion port with a job, use the 【19†SetInformationJobObject】 function with the job object information class JobObjectAssociateCompletionPortInformation and a pointer to a 【26†JOBOBJECT_ASSOCIATE_COMPLETION_PORT】 structure.
L71: It is best to do this when the job is inactive, to reduce the chance of missing notifications for processes whose states change during the association of the completion port.
L72: All messages are sent directly from the job as if the job had called the 【27†PostQueuedCompletionStatus】 function. A thread must monitor the completion port using the 【28†GetQueuedCompletionStatus】 function to pick up the messages. Note that, with the exception of limits set with the JobObjectNotificationLimitInformation information class, delivery of messages to the completion port is not guaranteed; failure of a message to arrive does not necessarily mean that the event did not occur.
L73: Notifications for limits set with JobObjectNotificationLimitInformation are guaranteed to arrive at the completion port. For a list of possible messages, see 【26†JOBOBJECT_ASSOCIATE_COMPLETION_PORT】.
L74: ## Resource Accounting for Jobs
L75: 
L76: The job object records basic accounting information for all its associated processes, including those that have terminated. To retrieve this accounting information, use the 【29†QueryInformationJobObject】 function. For a list of the accounting information that is maintained for a job, see the following topics:
L77: 
L78:   * 【30†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION】
L79:   * 【31†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_AND_IO_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION】
L80: If the job object is nested, accounting information for each child job is aggregated in its parent job. For more information, see 【13†Nested Jobs】.
L81: ## Managing Job Objects
L82: 
L83: The state of a job object is set to signaled when all of its processes are terminated because the specified end-of-job time limit has been exceeded. Use 【32†WaitForSingleObject】 or 【33†WaitForSingleObjectEx】 to monitor the job object for this event.
L84: 
L85: To obtain a handle for an existing job object, use the 【34†OpenJobObject】 function and specify the name given to the object when it was created. Only named job objects can be opened.
L86: To close a job object handle, use the 【35†CloseHandle】 function. The job is destroyed when its last handle has been closed and all associated processes have been terminated. However, if the job has the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE flag specified, closing the last job object handle terminates all associated processes and then destroys the job object itself.
L87: If a nested job has the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE flag specified, closing the last job object handle terminates all processes associated with the job and its child jobs in the hierarchy.
L88: ## Managing a Process Tree that Uses Job Objects
L89: 
L90: Starting with Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, an application can use 【13†nested jobs】 to manage a process tree that uses more than one job object. However, an application that must run on Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, or earlier versions of Windows that do not support nested jobs must manage the process tree in other ways.
L91: If a tool must manage a process tree that uses job objects and it is not possible to use nested jobs, both the tool and the members of the process tree must cooperate. Use one of the following options:
L92:   * Use the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. If the tool uses this limit, it cannot monitor an entire process tree. The tool can monitor only the processes it adds to the job. If these processes create child processes, they are not associated with the job. In this option, child processes can be associated with other job objects.
L93:   * Use the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. If the tool uses this limit, it can monitor the entire process tree, except for those processes that any member of the tree explicitly breaks away from the tree. A member of the tree can create a child process in a new job object by calling the 【15†CreateProcess】 function with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag, then calling the 【12†AssignProcessToJobObject】 function. Otherwise, the member must handle cases in which AssignProcessToJobObject fails.
L94: The CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag has no effect if the tree is not being monitored by the tool. Therefore, this is the preferred option, but it requires advance knowledge of the processes being monitored.
L95:   * Prevent breakaways of any kind by setting neither the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK nor the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. In this option, the tool can monitor the entire process tree. However, if a child process attempts to associate itself or another child process with a job by calling 【12†AssignProcessToJobObject】, the call will fail. If the process was designed to be associated with a specific job, this failure may prevent the process from working properly.
